checks.prompt: Four projects need speech recognition. (a) Subtitling a back catalogue of conference talks in nine languages. (b) Live captions on a video call, where anything above about half a second of lag is unacceptable. (c) A meeting tool that must label which of five participants said each sentence. (d) A safety-critical medical dictation tool where a fluent but wrong transcript would be worse than an empty one. Which is this model the default answer for, and what disqualifies it from each of the others?
checks.explanation: The model's home ground is offline, multilingual, robust transcription where a second or two of latency is fine — that is precisely the back-catalogue case. The three exclusions each come from a real property: the fixed thirty-second window makes streaming awkward rather than natural; speaker attribution is simply not something it does, and is a separate model's job; and its most notorious failure is hallucinating fluent text over silence or non-speech, which is exactly the failure mode a safety-critical setting cannot absorb.
options: (a). It is the no-questions-asked starting point for offline, multilingual, accuracy-over-latency transcription. (b) is disqualified because the model is built around a fixed thirty-second window, so naive use is batch rather than streaming and adds latency and boundary artefacts. (c) is disqualified because it does not attribute speech to speakers at all — that needs a separate diarisation model alongside it. (d) is the riskiest fit, because it will confidently invent fluent text over silence and non-speech
(b). Its encoder-decoder design streams naturally token by token, making it ideal for live captioning; the back catalogue is better served by a cloud service because of the language count
(c). Its timestamp tokens identify speakers as well as timing, which is what makes it a meeting tool; the other three are all better served by a smaller specialised model
(d). Because it was trained on an enormous weakly-supervised corpus, it abstains rather than guessing when the audio is unclear, which is exactly what a safety-critical setting needs

checks.prompt: Explain this model with the 'language model for audio' analogy: what does the encoder consume, what does the decoder produce, and how are they connected? Then explain the two ideas the notebook says make everything click, and use each to explain one practical consequence — one about how long files and live audio are handled, and one about how a single set of weights performs several different jobs.
checks.expected: A correct answer must describe the architecture: it is one sequence-to-sequence encoder-decoder transformer. The encoder consumes a fixed-size spectrogram image of the audio — the log-mel representation — after a convolutional stem, and produces audio hidden states. The decoder generates text tokens autoregressively, cross-attending to those audio states; it is next-token prediction exactly as in a text language model, over a vocabulary containing both words and control tokens. The first idea is the fixed window: the encoder always sees exactly thirty seconds, so shorter clips are zero-padded and longer audio must be sliced into thirty-second windows and stitched back together. The consequence must be drawn — long files are processed window by window, and live use is awkward because you either wait for a full window or cut words at boundaries, which is why streaming needs a wrapper doing chunking with overlap rather than the plain model. The second idea is that the task is a PROMPT rather than a model: transcribing, translating into English and identifying the language are all the same weights, selected by special tokens fed to the decoder before generation — a start marker, a language tag, a task tag, and a marker for whether timestamps are wanted. The consequence is that switching task or language costs nothing but different prompt tokens, and conversely that a wrong language tag — or a wrong auto-detection — steers the whole decode. A strong answer notes that the front end is deterministic signal processing with no learned weights, so everything before the encoder can be reproduced exactly.

checks.prompt: Somebody hand-builds the input features to feed the largest checkpoint directly, reusing code written for a small one, and gets a shape mismatch. They also want word-accurate timing for a subtitle tool and assume it comes free with the timestamps they already see. What are the two facts they are missing?
checks.explanation: Two independent facts. The feature dimension belongs to the checkpoint: the largest one expects 128 mel bins where the smaller ones expect 80, and if you build the features yourself the numbers have to line up — the frame count, set by the thirty-second window and the ten-millisecond hop, is the same either way. And timing has two tiers: segment-level timestamps fall out of the timestamp tokens and are cheap, while word-level timing requires cross-attention alignment that you ask for explicitly and pay for, or a dedicated forced-alignment tool when you need it tighter.
options: The number of mel bins is a property of the checkpoint — the largest one uses 128 where the smaller ones use 80 — so a hand-built front end must match the checkpoint it feeds; the number of frames is unchanged. And segment-level timing comes from timestamp tokens and is cheap, whereas word-level timing needs cross-attention alignment, requested explicitly at extra compute cost, or a separate forced-alignment tool for tighter results
The largest checkpoint uses a longer window rather than more mel bins, so the frame count differs; and word timing is free because every emitted token already carries its own timestamp
All checkpoints share one front end, so the mismatch must come from the sample rate; and word timing requires fine-tuning the model on aligned data
The mel bin count is chosen by the caller for any checkpoint as a speed-accuracy trade; and word timing is obtained by lowering the temperature so the decoder emits more timestamp tokens

checks.prompt: Reproduce the deterministic front end's arithmetic — no learned weights, no third-party libraries. Define `SR = 16000`, `N_FFT = 400`, `HOP = 160` and `CHUNK_SECONDS = 30`. Write `hz_to_mel(f)` as `2595 * log10(1 + f / 700)` and `mel_to_hz(m)` as its inverse. Write `pad_or_trim(audio, length)` returning a NEW list of exactly `length` values — the first `length` values when the input is at least that long, otherwise the input followed by `0.0` padding. Write `frame_count(samples, hop=HOP)` returning `samples // hop`, and `front_end_shape(n_mels=80, sr=SR, hop=HOP, seconds=CHUNK_SECONDS)` returning the `(n_mels, frames)` pair for one full window. Write `mel_filterbank(sr=SR, n_fft=N_FFT, n_mels=80)` returning a list of `n_mels` lists, each of length `n_fft // 2 + 1`: take `n_mels + 2` points spaced evenly on the mel scale from 0 to the mel value of `sr / 2`, convert each back to hertz and floor it to a bin index via `(n_fft + 1) * hz / sr`, then give filter `m` (1-based) a triangle rising linearly from 0 at `bins[m-1]` to 1 at `bins[m]` and falling back to 0 at `bins[m+1]`, clipping to the available width and guarding against a zero-width side. Write `normalize(energies)` implementing the final three steps on a flat list: take `log10` of each value clamped to a minimum of `1e-10`; then raise every value to at least the maximum minus 8; then return `(value + 4) / 4`. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The arithmetic at the top is the whole reason the window is a hard constraint rather than a default: thirty seconds at sixteen thousand samples per second, hopped every hundred and sixty samples, is exactly three thousand frames — so the encoder's input is a fixed-size image, everything shorter is padded into it and everything longer must be cut into windows by the caller. Note that changing the checkpoint changes the number of mel bins and leaves the frame count alone, which is exactly the shape mismatch people hit when they reuse front-end code across sizes. The filterbank assertions show what the mel scale buys: it is compressive, so equal steps in mel are small steps in hertz down low and large ones up high, which spends more filters where speech carries more information. And the last block is the dynamic-range floor — everything more than eight decades below the loudest bin is clamped, so a near-silent bin cannot stretch the scale, and the floor is relative, so making the whole clip quieter shifts the features rather than reshaping them.
checks.test:
import math

# The window is fixed: thirty seconds at the one sample rate the model accepts,
# and the ten-millisecond hop is what turns that into exactly three thousand frames.
assert SR * CHUNK_SECONDS == 480000
assert frame_count(480000) == 3000
assert HOP / SR == 0.01
assert front_end_shape() == (80, 3000)
# The largest checkpoint changes the number of mel bins and NOTHING else.
assert front_end_shape(n_mels=128) == (128, 3000)
assert front_end_shape(n_mels=80, seconds=30)[1] == front_end_shape(n_mels=128)[1]

# Anything shorter is zero-padded up to the window rather than processed as-is...
short = [0.5, -0.5, 0.25]
padded = pad_or_trim(short, 10)
assert len(padded) == 10, padded
assert padded[:3] == short and padded[3:] == [0.0] * 7, padded
# ...and anything longer is cut to it, which is why long audio has to be sliced
# into windows by the caller rather than handed over whole.
assert pad_or_trim(list(range(100)), 10) == list(range(10))
assert pad_or_trim([], 4) == [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
assert len(pad_or_trim([0.1] * 480000, 480000)) == 480000

# The mel scale is a monotonic warping of frequency that round-trips.
assert hz_to_mel(0) == 0.0
for hz in (100, 440, 1000, 4000, 8000):
    assert abs(mel_to_hz(hz_to_mel(hz)) - hz) < 1e-6, hz
assert hz_to_mel(200) < hz_to_mel(2000) < hz_to_mel(8000)
# It is compressive: doubling the frequency does not double the mel value, which is
# why low frequencies get proportionally more filters than high ones.
assert hz_to_mel(2000) < 2 * hz_to_mel(1000)
assert (mel_to_hz(1000) - mel_to_hz(900)) < (mel_to_hz(2000) - mel_to_hz(1900))

bank = mel_filterbank()
assert len(bank) == 80 and len(bank[0]) == N_FFT // 2 + 1 == 201

# Every filter is a triangle: non-negative, rising to a peak, then falling.
for index, filt in enumerate(bank):
    assert all(v >= 0.0 for v in filt), index
    peak = max(range(len(filt)), key=lambda k: filt[k])
    assert all(filt[k] <= filt[k + 1] + 1e-12 for k in range(peak)), index
    assert all(filt[k] >= filt[k + 1] - 1e-12 for k in range(peak, len(filt) - 1)), index
assert any(max(filt) > 0 for filt in bank)

# At this resolution the lowest few filters collapse to nothing, because several mel
# points floor to the same frequency bin -- an artefact of a 400-point transform.
active = [f for f in bank if max(f) > 0.0]
assert len(active) > len(bank) // 2, len(active)

# The filters march upward in frequency: each one's peak is at or above the last.
peaks = [max(range(len(f)), key=lambda k: f[k]) for f in active]
assert peaks == sorted(peaks), peaks
assert peaks[-1] > peaks[0]

# More bins means finer resolution over the SAME frequency range, not a wider one.
wide = mel_filterbank(n_mels=128)
assert len(wide) == 128 and len(wide[0]) == 201
assert max(range(len(wide[-1])), key=lambda k: wide[-1][k]) >= peaks[-1] - 2

# The log compresses energies spanning many orders of magnitude...
values = [1.0, 0.1, 0.01, 1e-4]
out = normalize(values)
assert all(out[i] > out[i + 1] for i in range(len(out) - 1)), out
assert abs(out[0] - 1.0) < 1e-9, out

# ...and the dynamic-range floor discards everything more than eight decades below
# the loudest bin, so near-silence cannot stretch the scale.
spread = normalize([1.0, 1e-20, 1e-30])
assert abs(spread[1] - spread[2]) < 1e-12, spread
assert abs(max(spread) - min(spread) - 2.0) < 1e-9, spread
assert abs(spread[0] - 1.0) < 1e-9, spread

# The floor is relative to the loudest value, so scaling everything shifts the
# result rather than changing its shape.
quiet = normalize([1e-6, 1e-7, 1e-8])
loud = normalize([1.0, 0.1, 0.01])
assert all(abs((loud[i] - quiet[i]) - 1.5) < 1e-9 for i in range(3)), (loud, quiet)

# A zero bin is clamped before the logarithm rather than producing infinity.
safe = normalize([1.0, 0.0])
assert all(math.isfinite(v) for v in safe), safe
assert abs(safe[1] - safe[0] + 2.0) < 1e-9, safe

checks.prompt: A batch transcription job produces three kinds of bad output: on files that begin with thirty seconds of music, the entire transcript is in the wrong language; on long files, one bad passage is followed by pages of the same sentence repeated; and on quiet recordings, stretches of silence come back as short polite phrases and what look like subtitle credits. What causes each, and what mitigates it?
checks.explanation: Three separate and well-documented failure modes. Language identification looks only at the first window, so whatever opens the file decides the language for all of it — state the language when you know it. Repetition is the decoder getting stuck; the temperature fallback usually breaks it, and conditioning each window on the previous text is what lets a single bad window contaminate the rest. And confident text over silence is the model's signature hallucination, complete with phrases baked in from its training data — the practical defences are voice-activity detection before transcription and checking the per-segment no-speech probability and average log-probability.
options: Language identification runs on the FIRST window only, so an opening of music or another language misdetects the whole file — pass the language explicitly when you know it. The repetition is the decoder looping, which the built-in temperature fallback usually breaks and which is made worse by conditioning each window on the previous text, since one bad window then poisons everything after it — turning that conditioning off helps. And the invented phrases on silence are the model's known hallucination behaviour, learnt from its training data — run voice-activity detection first and check the reported no-speech probability and average log-probability
All three indicate the audio was not resampled correctly; forcing the required rate and channel count before decoding resolves the language detection, the repetition and the invented phrases together

The wrong language means the language tag was omitted so the model defaulted to its most common training language; the repetition is a beam-search artefact fixed by greedy decoding; and the invented phrases mean the file contains inaudible speech that a larger checkpoint would recover

The wrong language and the repetition are both caused by window boundaries cutting words, fixed by overlapping the windows; the invented phrases are an artefact of timestamp tokens and disappear when timestamps are disabled

checks.prompt: Four alternatives are on the table alongside the reference implementation: a re-implementation on a faster inference runtime, an alignment-and-diarisation wrapper, a C++ port for on-device use, and a managed cloud service. Say what each buys and costs. Then advise two teams: one transcribing ten thousand hours of archive audio on their own hardware, and one building a podcast tool that must show who said what with word-accurate highlighting. State the rule of thumb you are applying.
checks.expected: A correct answer must cover all four alternatives. The faster re-implementation on an optimised inference runtime gives several times the throughput and much lower memory, plus built-in voice-activity detection, at the cost of being a separate library and model format. The alignment-and-diarisation wrapper gives word-accurate timestamps through forced alignment and speaker attribution by pairing with a diarisation model, at the cost of a heavier install and more dependencies. The C++ port gives on-device and edge operation with quantised weights and no Python runtime, at the cost of a native build and fewer knobs. The managed cloud service gives scale, real-time interfaces, diarisation and service guarantees, at the cost of per-minute charges, data leaving your machine and vendor lock-in. The advice must match the constraints: ten thousand hours on your own hardware is a throughput and memory problem, so the faster runtime is the answer, and the reference implementation is the correctness baseline rather than the production engine. The podcast tool needs word-accurate timing AND speaker attribution, neither of which the base model provides, so the alignment-and-diarisation wrapper — or the base model paired with a separate diarisation model — is the answer. The rule of thumb must be stated: reach for this model first for offline, multilingual, accuracy-over-latency transcription; move to the faster runtime the moment throughput or memory matters; move to the alignment wrapper when precise word timing or speaker attribution is required; and move to a streaming or cloud option only when sub-second latency is non-negotiable.
